I recommend selling Plant 6 to a buyer for $37.5 million. The plant lost $9.0 million after corporate costs, and its underlying cost base sits $32.9 million above what the Company's average margin would imply, so the business has no path to profitability at its current volume. Retooling would cost $30.0 million up front to improve operating income by $7.5 million a year, which leaves the first four quarters at a net cash loss of roughly $22 million and a shortfall against the one-year objective. Closing would add $16.5 million a year to operating income, but it costs $10.0 million to move equipment, plus severance and relocation, and the moved positions are only partly filled, so its first-year net is only about $6 million before those costs. Selling gives the most value within four quarters: the proceeds of $37.5 million more than offset the loss of $15.3 million a year in operating income, and the sale is funded from the $444.9 million of available liquidity.

Employees: the buyer has committed to keep 171 of the 190 positions for at least two years, so I have allocated those people to transfer with the plant. The remaining 19 positions are not covered, and I have offered them positions at the other plants. Management expects only about 15% of such offers to be accepted, so most of those 19 are likely to be separated, at a severance cost of about $4,566 each, which is immaterial to the decision. Relocation support of $20,000 per accepting employee applies only to those who move.

The Company keeps the corporate costs of $24.3 million a year allocated to the plant, which is a continuing drag that should be addressed in the overhead review. Sale proceeds should be applied to the balance sheet, with the dividend and repurchase plan reviewed against the lower operating income.

I chose to sell Plant 6, with its product family, to a buyer. This gives the largest one-year value of the three options. The sale brings in $37.5 million once. Operating income falls by $15.3 million a year, because $24.3 million of the corporate costs allocated to the plant stays with the Company, but the plant's loss of $9.0 million after corporate costs leaves the Company. Over the next four quarters the net effect is about +$22 million before severance, against about +$6.5 million for closing and about -$22.5 million for retooling. Retooling costs $30.0 million up front and needs 162 of the 190 positions, so its payback is slower than the one-year horizon allows. Closing costs $10.0 million and gains $16.5 million a year, which is positive but smaller than the sale's first-year value.

On people, the buyer takes 171 positions for at least two years, so those employees keep their jobs and no severance is paid on them. I offer the remaining 19 positions at the other plants, which need workers and hire about 500 people a year. Those moves avoid severance and external hiring, and the 19 people are within the 29 available places. Management expects about 15% of offers to be accepted, so some of these 19 may decline, and I will report the outcome. No one is eliminated in this plan.

The sale is conditional on the buyer keeping the staff. Its cash proceeds sit well within the $444.9 million of available liquidity. The main risk is that the buyer does not keep the 171 roles beyond two years, which would affect later periods but not this year's value.

I recommend closing Plant 6 and moving its product family to the other plants. Of the three options, closing gives the largest recurring gain to operating income: $16.5M a year, permanently. Its one-time cost is $10.0M for moving equipment, which is recovered in roughly seven months at the run-rate gain. Selling reduces operating income by $15.3M a year because $24.3M of allocated corporate cost stays behind; the $37.5M proceeds do not offset a permanent annual reduction. Retooling needs $30.0M of capital for $7.5M a year, a payback of about four years, and it still leaves 28 people without a role.

The Company's available liquidity of $444.9M covers the $10.0M closing cost plus severance and relocation, with ample room to spare. Relocation to other plants is limited to 29 people, the most management expects to accept, at $20,000 each. Those 29 are moved into positions at the other plants, which need 190 positions in total and would otherwise be filled by outside hiring. The remaining 161 roles are eliminated, with severance of about $4,566 per person on average. Those employees are not needed once the product family is made elsewhere, and the other plants' open positions are filled by the planned hiring of about 500 people a year, so retaining the surplus local staff at a plant that is closing would add cost without benefit.

The decision is about value for shareholders over the next four quarters. Closing delivers the largest improvement in operating income, the smallest one-time outlay relative to that gain, and no dependence on the buyer's behavior or on capital spending at a loss-making site. The main risks are execution of the transfer of product lines and the assumption that about half of the above-average cost is removed; these should be monitored closely through the year.
